subject: science
title: Understand states of matter and evaporation
promise: This starts from the three states and the exact words for moving between them — melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing — then answers the question this topic really turns on: where does a puddle GO?

sections.heading: Three states, one substance
sections.body:
Water is the star witness of this topic because you have met it in all three states: solid ice, liquid water, and water vapour — a gas hiding invisibly in the air.
It is the SAME substance in each state. Nothing is added and nothing is taken away when ice melts into water; the water has simply changed how it holds itself. That is what a CHANGE OF STATE is: the same stuff, behaving a different way.
Solids keep their shape. Liquids flow and take their container's shape. Gases spread out to fill whatever space they can find.
sections.example: An ice cube, the puddle it melts into, and the vapour that puddle becomes are all the same water.

sections.heading: Melting and freezing: crossing 0°C
sections.body:
MELTING is solid turning to liquid; FREEZING is liquid turning back to solid. They are the same doorway crossed in opposite directions, and for water that doorway sits at 0 degrees Celsius.
Warm ice above 0°C and it melts; cool water below 0°C and it freezes. The temperature where this happens is called the MELTING POINT, and every substance has its own — chocolate's is close to body heat (which is why it melts in your hand), and iron's is over 1,500°C.
sections.example: Butter melts in a warm pan and hardens again in the fridge — the same doorway, crossed both ways.

sections.heading: Boiling and evaporating are not the same thing
sections.body:
Both turn liquid into gas, but they are different events.
BOILING happens only at the boiling point — 100°C for water — and it happens throughout the liquid: the whole kettle churns with bubbles of vapour.
EVAPORATION happens at ANY temperature, and only at the SURFACE. A puddle at 20°C is nowhere near boiling, yet it still disappears — its surface water escapes into the air as vapour, a little at a time.
That is where puddles, wet washing and shrinking ponds go: not into the ground, but into the air.
sections.example: Wet washing dries on a cold day. It never boils — its water evaporates from the surface, thread by thread.

sections.heading: What makes evaporation faster
sections.body:
Three things speed evaporation up, and you can see all three at work on a washing line.
WARMTH: warm water evaporates faster than cold — washing dries quicker on a sunny day.
WIND: moving air carries the escaped vapour away and brings drier air in — washing dries quicker on a breezy day.
SPREAD: the more surface, the more escape routes — washing spread out dries quicker than washing in a heap, and a shallow wide puddle beats a deep narrow one.
Warm, windy, spread out: the recipe for fast drying.
sections.example: The same spilt water dries in minutes as a thin film across the table, but takes hours as a deep pool in a cup.

sections.heading: Condensation: the return journey
sections.body:
CONDENSATION is evaporation's opposite: gas turning back into liquid, which happens when water vapour meets something COLD.
Breathe on a cold window and it mists over — the vapour in your warm breath condenses on the cold glass. A cold drink on a warm day grows droplets on the outside; that water was not leaking through the glass, it condensed out of the air.
Evaporation up, condensation down: together they run the WATER CYCLE — sea water evaporates, rises, condenses into clouds, and falls again as rain.
sections.example: The mirror mists over after a hot shower: shower vapour condensing on the cooler glass.

mistakes.wrong: Saying a puddle "soaks away into the air" only on hot days, because water needs to boil to become a gas.
mistakes.right: Evaporation happens at ANY temperature, from the surface — cold puddles disappear too, just more slowly.
mistakes.why: Boiling needs 100°C; evaporation does not. Confusing the two makes half of everyday drying impossible to explain.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking the droplets on a cold drink leaked through the glass.
mistakes.right: They CONDENSED there — water vapour in the air turned liquid on meeting the cold surface.
mistakes.why: Glass is waterproof. The water came from the air outside the glass, not the drink inside it.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking ice becomes a different substance when it melts.
mistakes.right: Melting changes the STATE, not the substance — ice, water and water vapour are all the same water.
mistakes.why: A change of state is reversible precisely because nothing was added or taken away; freeze the water and the ice is back.

check.question: At what temperature does water freeze?
check.explanation: Water's freezing and melting point is 0°C — the same doorway crossed in opposite directions.

check.question: At what temperature does water boil?
check.explanation: Water boils at 100°C, turning to vapour throughout the liquid, not just at the surface.

check.question: What is EVAPORATION?
options: Liquid turning to gas at the surface, at any temperature
check.answer: Liquid turning to gas at the surface, at any temperature
check.explanation: Evaporation is the surface escape of liquid into gas — no boiling required.

check.question: Where does a drying puddle's water GO?
options: Into the air as water vapour
check.answer: Into the air as water vapour
check.explanation: The surface water evaporates into the air as invisible vapour — the same water, in its gas state.

check.question: Which washing line dries clothes FASTEST?
options: A warm, windy day with clothes spread out
A cold, still day with clothes in a heap
A warm day with clothes folded in a pile
A windy day with clothes rolled up
check.answer: A warm, windy day with clothes spread out
check.explanation: Warmth, moving air and a large surface are the three accelerators of evaporation — this option has all three.

check.question: What is CONDENSATION?
options: Gas turning back into liquid on something cold
check.answer: Gas turning back into liquid on something cold
check.explanation: Condensation is evaporation's reverse — vapour meets a cold surface and turns liquid, like mist on a cold window.

check.question: Why do droplets form on the OUTSIDE of a cold drink?
options: Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold glass
The drink leaks through the glass
check.answer: Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold glass
check.explanation: The air always carries invisible vapour; the cold surface turns it back to liquid.

check.question: How are boiling and evaporation DIFFERENT?
options: Boiling needs the boiling point and happens throughout; evaporation happens at any temperature, at the surface
They are the same thing with two names
check.answer: Boiling needs the boiling point and happens throughout; evaporation happens at any temperature, at the surface
check.explanation: That difference is why cold puddles still disappear — no boiling required.

check.question: Ice melts into water. What has changed?
options: Only its state — it is the same substance
It has become a new substance
check.answer: Only its state — it is the same substance
check.explanation: A change of state rearranges the same stuff — freeze it again and the ice returns.

check.question: Which sequence describes the water cycle?
options: Evaporate, rise, condense into cloud, fall as rain
check.answer: Evaporate, rise, condense into cloud, fall as rain
check.explanation: Water evaporates from seas and lakes, condenses into clouds where the air is cold, and returns as rain.

practice.prompt: Name the three states of matter, using water as the example.
practice.hint: You have seen water in all three.

practice.prompt: What is it called when a solid turns into a liquid?
What is it called when a gas turns back into a liquid on a cold surface?
practice.hint: It mists up a cold window.

practice.prompt: Does a puddle need to boil to disappear? Explain in one sentence.
practice.answer: No — its water evaporates from the surface at any temperature.
practice.hint: What is the difference between boiling and evaporating?

practice.prompt: Give the three things that speed up evaporation.
practice.answer: Warmth, moving air (wind), and a larger spread-out surface.
practice.hint: Think of what dries washing fastest.

practice.prompt: Why does a shallow, wide puddle dry faster than a deep, narrow one holding the same water?
practice.answer: It has a much larger surface, and evaporation only happens at the surface — more surface, more escape routes.

practice.prompt: A mirror mists over after a hot shower. Name the process and explain it.
practice.answer: Condensation — the shower's water vapour turns back to liquid on the cooler mirror surface.
practice.hint: Warm vapour is meeting cold glass.

practice.prompt: Chocolate melts in your hand but iron does not. What does this tell you about their melting points?
practice.answer: Chocolate's melting point is low (near body temperature); iron's is far higher — every substance has its own melting point.
practice.hint: The doorway temperature differs from substance to substance.

practice.prompt: Frost forms overnight, then vanishes in the morning sun without leaving the grass wet. Which changes of state happened to the water on that grass?
practice.answer: Water froze into frost overnight, then melted and evaporated (some frost can even go straight to vapour) as it warmed.
practice.hint: Cross the doorways one at a time: night cold, then morning warmth.

practice.prompt: Explain how the sea, the sun, the sky and the rain form one continuous cycle.
practice.answer: The sun warms the sea so water evaporates; the vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds; the drops grow heavy and fall as rain, running back to the sea.
practice.hint: Evaporation up, condensation in the cold sky, then the return journey.

practice.prompt: Two identical bowls of water sit in the same room, one covered with cling film. A week later, which holds more water and why?
practice.answer: The covered one — the film traps the vapour so it cannot escape (much of it condenses and drips back), while the open bowl loses water to the air.
practice.hint: Evaporation needs an escape route to the open air.

practice.prompt: Why is it WRONG to say wet washing 'boils dry' on the line?
practice.answer: Boiling only happens at 100°C throughout the liquid; the washing is nowhere near that — its water evaporates from the surface at ordinary temperature.
practice.hint: Which of the two liquid-to-gas processes works at any temperature?
